chapters.title: Chapter 3: When Country Risk Turns Into Crisis

lessons.title: The IMF's Role: Bailouts, Conditionality, and What a Programme Actually Requires

children.text: When a country runs out of reserves, cannot roll over its debt, and cannot defend its currency any further, exactly the Stage 4 crisis point from earlier in this chapter, it has very few places left to turn. The International Monetary Fund exists precisely for this moment. This closing lesson of the chapter covers what an IMF programme actually is, what a country has to promise to get one, and why that promise, called conditionality, is simultaneously what makes these programmes work and what makes them so politically explosive.

markDefs.definition: Financial support extended by the IMF to a member country facing a balance of payments crisis, funded from a pool of contributions (quotas) made by the IMF's over 190 member countries, and disbursed in tranches tied to the country meeting agreed policy commitments.

children.text: The IMF is not a charity, and it is not simply handing out free money. It is a member-owned institution, funded by contributions, called quotas, from its over 190 member countries, that acts as a lender of last resort for countries facing a balance of payments crisis, meaning they cannot access enough foreign currency through normal trade and investment channels to meet their external obligations. An
provides that country with foreign currency, in stages, in exchange for a set of policy commitments designed to fix the underlying problem, not just paper over it.

Deeper, structural balance of payments problems requiring longer reform, the type Sri Lanka used

children.text: Conditionality: The Price of the Loan

markDefs.definition: The set of policy commitments a country agrees to as a condition of receiving IMF financing, with money released in tranches only as the country meets agreed targets and reform steps.

children.text: IMF money does not arrive as one lump sum. It is released in tranches, and each tranche is conditional on the country meeting specific commitments, collectively called

. These commitments typically fall into three categories: prior actions, specific steps a government must complete before the IMF's Board even approves the programme, to demonstrate genuine commitment upfront; performance criteria, quantitative targets, like a maximum fiscal deficit or a minimum level of reserves, checked at each periodic review; and structural benchmarks, reform steps with deadlines, such as passing a specific tax law or restructuring a loss-making state enterprise. Miss enough of these, and the next tranche of funding is delayed or withheld entirely, which is exactly the leverage that makes conditionality effective, and controversial.

Sri Lanka's own Extended Fund Facility, approved in March 2023, is a clear real-world example of what conditionality actually asks a country to do. Conditions included raising the VAT rate, broadening the income tax base, moving toward cost-reflective pricing for electricity and fuel (ending subsidies that had been drawing down reserves), and completing a debt restructuring with both bondholders and official creditors, alongside a first-of-its-kind IMF governance diagnostic assessing corruption vulnerabilities in the country's public institutions.

body.title: The Case For and Against IMF Conditionality

columns.label: The Case For
points: Ensures the country actually addresses the root causes of the crisis, not just borrows time
Protects the IMF's own revolving pool of member funds, so it remains available for the next country in crisis
A credible programme often catalyses the return of other lenders and investors, who take IMF approval as a signal of a credible reform path
Provides an external anchor that can help a government push through reforms it might struggle to justify domestically on its own

columns.label: The Case Against
points: Austerity measures, tax hikes, subsidy cuts, often hit the poorest households hardest and fastest, well before growth benefits, if any, materialise
Critics point to past programmes, especially during the 1997-98 Asian Financial Crisis, as having been too rigid, deepening recessions rather than easing them
Conditions can be seen as external interference in a sovereign country's own domestic policy choices
Governments implementing IMF-mandated tax hikes or subsidy cuts often face real political backlash, exactly what continued in Sri Lanka even after its 2023 programme began

children.text: India is not exempt from this history. Recall from Chapter 1 that India's external debt reached around 19% of GDP by 1991, and the same year, India faced its own acute balance of payments crisis: reserves fell so low they could barely cover a few weeks of imports. India approached the IMF for a loan, and in a moment now etched into Indian economic folklore, physically pledged gold reserves, flown to the Bank of England and the Union Bank of Switzerland as collateral, to secure emergency foreign currency while the IMF programme was arranged. The conditionality attached to that support, and the reforms India undertook alongside it, currency devaluation, industrial delicensing, and trade liberalisation, are widely credited as the starting point of the economic reforms that reshaped India's growth trajectory over the following decades.

body.text: India's 1991 experience is a useful counterpoint to Sri Lanka's more recent one. Both faced genuine balance of payments crises requiring IMF support and painful conditionality. India's episode is now generally remembered as a catalyst for reforms that unlocked decades of growth, while Sri Lanka's outcome is still being written. The difference is not that conditionality was gentler in one case. It has more to do with how each country's institutions, political will, and broader economic starting point shaped what came after the programme.

body.title: The Politician's Dilemma
body.scenario: A finance minister is negotiating an IMF Extended Fund Facility during an acute currency and reserves crisis. The IMF's proposed conditions include raising fuel prices to cost-reflective levels (ending a subsidy that keeps the price artificially low) and cutting a popular rural income support scheme by 30%. Elections are eighteen months away, and the minister knows these measures will be deeply unpopular.
body.prompt: What is the underlying trade-off the minister actually faces here, beyond just short-term political popularity?
body.modelAnswer: The trade-off is between short-term political pain and continued access to the foreign currency the country needs to avoid a disorderly default and the much larger economic and social damage that would follow, the kind of shortages and instability covered earlier in this chapter's Sri Lanka case study. Refusing the IMF's conditions to protect popularity in the short run does not remove the underlying balance of payments problem, it just removes the financing that could help manage it, likely forcing an even harder, less controlled adjustment later, through capital controls, a disorderly currency collapse, or default. The minister's real choice is between a managed, externally financed adjustment now, with real political cost, or an unmanaged one later, usually with even greater economic and political cost.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why does the IMF release programme funding in tranches instead of as a single upfront disbursement?
options: To earn additional interest on the undisbursed portion
To give itself leverage to ensure the country actually follows through on agreed reforms, since future tranches depend on meeting prior commitments
Because IMF rules require all loans to be repaid before further funds can be released
Tranche-based disbursement is a historical accident with no functional purpose today
body.explanation: Releasing funds in stages, tied to meeting performance criteria and structural benchmarks, gives the IMF ongoing leverage throughout the programme. If a country stalls on its commitments, the next tranche can be withheld, which is precisely the mechanism, conditionality, that is meant to ensure a programme actually addresses the underlying crisis rather than simply providing a one-time cash infusion that gets spent without real reform.

body.text: An IMF programme is not free money and not a punishment. It is a conditional bridge: foreign currency now, in exchange for a country doing the hard reforms it likely needed to do anyway, just under a deadline and with real consequences for missing it.

children.text: This closes out how country risk actually turns into crisis, and how a country claws its way back out. The final chapter turns the lens back toward you as an investor: how foreign institutional investors actually price country risk before putting money into India, why emerging market bonds pay the extra yield they do, and how to build your own practical country risk checklist for looking at any market beyond your own.

points: The IMF is a member-funded lender of last resort for countries facing balance of payments crises, not a source of unconditional free money.
IMF facilities range from short-term Stand-By Arrangements to longer Extended Fund Facilities for deeper structural problems, to emergency Rapid Financing Instruments for sudden shocks.
Conditionality, prior actions, performance criteria, and structural benchmarks, ties fund disbursement in tranches to a country actually meeting agreed reform commitments.

Conditionality is genuinely double-edged: it protects the IMF's resources and can catalyse a credible reform path, but its austerity-style measures often hit the poorest hardest and generate real political backlash, as seen in Sri Lanka.

India's own 1991 IMF episode, including its famous gold collateral pledge, is widely seen as the catalyst for the reforms that reshaped India's growth path, a reminder that IMF programmes can be a genuine turning point, not only a crisis marker.

body.text: The programme details, dates, and figures in this lesson, including Sri Lanka's 2023 EFF conditions and India's 1991 episode, are drawn from widely reported historical and public IMF sources and simplified for teaching purposes. For precise programme terms, consult the IMF's own country programme documents and press releases directly.
